projects.name: The years between us
projects.shortDesc: A bachelor's thesis on how war experiences persist across generations — as an interactive app and an analogue card game.
projects.desc:
Between Us, the Years explores how war experiences continue to shape family relationships, attitudes, and silence across generations, even without being consciously remembered.

The thesis combines an interactive digital application, built around scroll and non-linear movement instead of linear reading, with an analogue card game. Its central rule — every drawn card must be passed on, though reacting to it stays voluntary — turns passing-on and silence into something players actually enact.
projects.caption:
The thesis draws on psychoanalytic and social-science approaches to the transgenerational transmission of war experiences, treating memory as social and relational rather than individually stored — passed on through attitudes, affects, and relational patterns rather than concrete content.

The digital application is built from six sections of five chapters each, thirty in total, navigated through scroll and click interaction, conditional logic, and camera movement rather than page-turning — replacing linear reading with a rhythm of movement, pause, and interruption.

Each of the application's thirty chapters is mapped to one of the card game's thirty cards. The game's central rule is that every drawn card must be passed on, while reacting to it is voluntary; points mark where connection occurs rather than rewarding openness or performance, and silence is neither punished nor rewarded.

Development began with research into memory and transgenerational transmission, then continued directly in the digital medium — structure, interaction, and content built in parallel rather than in sequence — while the card game was developed alongside it as an independent, coordinated format.

projects.name: ONDRA
projects.shortDesc: An interactive digital world making the human impact on climate change and the water cycle experienceable, zone by zone.
projects.desc:
ondra is a digital companion piece to the book Energiewende verstehen, developed because climate change and the energy transition are often perceived as too abstract or overwhelming.

Users move through an abstracted world of distinct climatic zones at their own pace. The design follows the logic of a game without its competitive or reward mechanics — interaction serves orientation and understanding, not performance.
projects.caption:
Gamification functions here as a knowledge-mediation strategy rather than a motivational device: complex ecological relationships are made experienceable through action, with a focus on how individual choices are embedded in larger climatic processes. Following current shifts in climate communication from guilt toward individual efficacy, the project surfaces small, realistic possibilities for action rather than moral pressure.

Each climatic zone is built as its own experiential space, conveying knowledge about atmosphere, movement, and interaction through a clear colour and zone concept that supports intuitive navigation.

Research drew on IPCC reports and publications from the German Federal Environment Agency and NASA, condensed into the core relationships and everyday actions suited to playful mediation. A spatial and narrative concept then translated this research into the different climate zones, structured through a storyboard, with visuals, sound, and interaction developed and tested iteratively alongside it.

projects.name: all the water above me came from below
projects.shortDesc: A multimedia project using the myth of Ino's transformation to question the fashion-photography "male gaze."
projects.desc:
All the water above me came from below combines photography, experimental film, text, and sound with theoretical research into visual representations of femininity in fashion photography.

It functions as both a website and an exhibition concept: an open, non-linear space where photographic works, film excerpts, text, and audio sit equally side by side, without a single prescribed reading.
projects.caption:
The project draws on three references: Laura Mulvey's concept of the male gaze, describing women shown from a male-dominated, objectifying perspective; Jacques Derrida's deconstruction, which treats meaning as unstable and context-dependent rather than fixed; and the mythological figure of Ino, whose leap into the sea stands not for an ending but for a moment of radical uncertainty and transformation.

Rather than showing women as static image objects, the work moves the state of transition into focus — the male gaze is irritated through instability and ambivalence rather than illustrated directly, with the myth serving as a thinking model rather than a narrative motif.

Work began with research into feminist film theory and photographic references including Helmut Newton and Horst P. Horst, producing a moodboard of visual states — blur, movement, suspension, dissolution — and a storyboard that organises transitions rather than a linear narrative, deliberately leaving beginning and end open.

projects.name: BTS
projects.shortDesc: An interactive spatial installation visualising how an AI system makes decisions, built with the Fraunhofer Institute.
projects.desc:
BTS is an interdisciplinary collaboration between Hochschule München and the Fraunhofer Institute for Cognitive Systems (IKS), developing a design-based approach to AI that is experienced spatially rather than explained technically.

The installation forgoes interfaces and diagrams in favour of spatial dramaturgy: transparent materials, light, projection, and movement make the AI's processes traceable without fully disclosing them, balancing control and openness.
projects.caption:
Visitors move through a spatial sequence structured around input, processing, and output — the three stages of an AI system — using interactive inputs and filters to influence it directly and observe how their changes affect the results. The installation follows a principle of learning by doing: understanding arises through action and observation rather than explanation.

The project was carried out by a five-person team — Jakob Sikeler, Lorenz Stanislaus, Michelle Walter, Azim Alizada, and Alina Schröder — in cooperation between Hochschule München and the Fraunhofer Institute for Cognitive Systems (IKS).

projects.name: From Augsburg to Lothstraße
projects.shortDesc: A collection of observations made during train rides between Augsburg and Lothstraße, gathered on a website.
projects.desc: The project is based on participant observation: things noticed during the recurring train commute — often while bored — were written down as they occurred and later collected on this website.

projects.name: Interactive poster
projects.shortDesc: An interactive poster controlled with a keyboard — pressing different keys triggers something on the poster.
projects.desc: The poster responds to keyboard input: different keys trigger different reactions on the poster. There's no set instruction for what to press — the piece works through trying keys out and seeing what happens.
